messages.subject: Sample size question?
messages.subject_clean: Sample size question?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am a beginner with SEM and lavaan. So, I am really sorry that my questions may seem dumb.
I am running quite a complex model. It has 485 free parameters and 37 equality constraints. I have a sample of 207 observations (or units). My data is longitudinal with two time points. So, in total, I have 414 data points.
When I ran the model, everything looks fine. It converged to a solution and the global fitness indices seem fine. The only warning I received is:

"In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative"

In fact, I have only 2 latent variables in the model and the variance of one of them is negative.

So:
1) Can anyone help me figure out how to deal with the warning above? Is it serious? I mean given that the model converges to a solution and the fitness indices are fine, what the implication of the warning could be? Is it related to the sample size?
2) Will my sample size be an issue for publication, given that the are more parameters than observations (or units) in my model?

Thank you so much,

Ranaivo

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel SEM, level 2 model, standard errors are all NA..
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel SEM, level 2 model, standard errors are all NA..
messages.body_plain:
> Q1. If I want to test level 2 only, what should I do?
>
> I found an instruction about having level 1 model only (below) from your homepage but not sure how to do in my case..

Do you have a multiple-indicator measurement model at level 2?  Since you measured it on several occasions, and your N is too small to use the standard longitudinal CFA (with occasions in wide format), you would need to specify the same measurement model at both levels, with equal factor loadings across levels.  This follows from the assumption that you are measuring the same person-level construct at each occasion.  See here for a discussion about this in the context of subjects nested in groups/clusters:

https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01640/full

> Q2. The reason why I’m asking this question is because I got the following warning messages about all my within-person indicators for some individuals(clusters):
>
> Level-1 variable “r1” has no variance within some clusters. The cluster ids with zero within variance are: A1, …
>
> Level-1 variable “r2” has no variance within some clusters. The cluster ids with zero within variance are: A1, …

It looks like those are constant within each subject whose cluster ID is listed in the message (A1, ...).  If they are constant within all subjects, then they are Level-2 variables only, so they should not appear in your Level-1 model.

Posting your syntax would make it easier to provide more informative advice.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I m trying to stimulate a 4-Likert cat dataset i receive this error when I m adding the thresholds statements

Not sure if this is the reason for the error, but why are you specifying both residual variances AND scaling factors (with the ~*~ operator)?  One implies the other.  I would omit the scaling factors (which don't have population values anyway) and just leave your residual variances in there (which do have population values).  And perhaps you would have to set parameterization = "theta" too?

>    SE=~RI
>    ET=~RI
>    RI=~PG
>    SE=~PG
>    ET=~PG

Is there a reason you are thinking of RI & PG as indicators of SE and ET (and RI)?  All of those factors have observed indicators.  Second-order loadings are just in the Beta matrix, and it is arbitrary to just define the regression paths instead.  Try doing this, in case that is throwing lavaan's expectations off:

RI ~ SE + ET
PG ~ RI + SE + ET

But remember to specify population values for those slopes, don't just leave the parameters "blank".

> ! means
>   ET+RI+PG+ SE~1*1;
>   x1+x2+x3+x4+x5+x6+x7+x8+x9+x10+x11+x12+x13~1*1;
>   y1+y2+y3+y4+y5+y6+y7+y8+y9+y10+y11+y12+y13+y14+y15+y16+y17~1*1;

Do you realize you are setting your latent means to 1 instead of 0?  There's nothing actually wrong with that, but you would not be able to recover the other population parameters because the intercepts of latent item-responses are fixed to zero for identification when estimating the model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I have no idea what's wrong with syntax.

The problem is when you don't assign a different name to the object used to store the sem() results.

Model3a <- sem(Model3a, ...)

So when you pass Model3a (also Model3b) to eqMI.main(), it gives you the error that a lavaan object (of S4 class) cannot be coerced to a character vector (which is what your model syntax must be).

messages.subject: Re: Sample size question?
messages.subject_clean: Sample size question?
messages.body_plain:
> I have a sample of 207 observations (or units). My data is longitudinal with two time points. So, in total, I have 414 data points.

Not if your data are in wide format.  Then you would still have N=207 but twice as many variables (2 occasions).  If you are storing your occasions in long format, you are violating your independence assumption, unless you use ML-SEM with persons as clusters.

> "In lav_object_post_check(object) :
>   lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative"
>
> In fact, I have only 2 latent variables in the model and the variance of one of them is negative.
>
> So:
> 1) Can anyone help me figure out how to deal with the warning above? Is it serious?

I don't understand your question.  You yourself verified that the message is correct: you have 2 latent variables, one of their variance estimates was negative.

> I mean given that the model converges to a solution and the fitness indices are fine, what the implication of the warning could be? Is it related to the sample size?

Variances can be estimated as negative because of gross model misspecification (apparently not the case here?) or just due to sampling error.  It will happen more often the closer the true parameter is to zero and the smaller the sample is.  You can check whether the interval estimate includes positive values, in which case you can't reject the H0 that the true variance is nonnegative:

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

> 2) Will my sample size be an issue for publication, given that the are more parameters than observations (or units) in my model?

Frankly, I think it should be.  To have any confidence in so many simultaneously estimated parameters, you need enough data to support it.  Using insufficient samples is one of the (many) root causes of the replicability crisis.  It is not just that your Type II error rate is high (low power), but when you make Type I errors, the estimated effect size must by definition be quite large to have been (incorrectly) flagged as significant.  Or even if there really is an effect, detecting it as significant will only happen when it is over estimated to a large degree, which makes it harder to trust even meta-analyses that accumulate information filtered by publication bias, etc.

Is it possible to isolate particular hypotheses you want to test, that could be addressed with reduced models of a subset of variables at a time?  Sharing your syntax would help provide more well-informed advice.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
The error Terrence brought your attention to was that you replaced Model3b (the syntax) with Model3b (the lavaan object that is the result of the sem() call). So the syntax is no longer available when you get to the eqMI calls.

So change:

Model3b<- sem(Model3b, data = Estudios_de_Aceptacion_UPR_2020, meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "MLR", mimic = "Mplus")

to

Model3b.fitted <- sem(Model3b, data = Estudios_de_Aceptacion_UPR_2020, meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "MLR", mimic = "Mplus")

On Sunday, November 1, 2020 at 6:04:59 AM UTC-5 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I have a sample of 207 observations (or units). My data is longitudinal with two time points. So, in total, I have 414 data points.
>
> Not if your data are in wide format.  Then you would still have N=207 but twice as many variables (2 occasions).  If you are storing your occasions in long format, you are violating your independence assumption, unless you use ML-SEM with persons as clusters.
>
> > "In lav_object_post_check(object) :
> >   lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative"
> >
> > In fact, I have only 2 latent variables in the model and the variance of one of them is negative.
> >
> > So:
> > 1) Can anyone help me figure out how to deal with the warning above? Is it serious?
>
> I don't understand your question.  You yourself verified that the message is correct: you have 2 latent variables, one of their variance estimates was negative.
>
> > I mean given that the model converges to a solution and the fitness indices are fine, what the implication of the warning could be? Is it related to the sample size?
>
> Variances can be estimated as negative because of gross model misspecification (apparently not the case here?) or just due to sampling error.  It will happen more often the closer the true parameter is to zero and the smaller the sample is.  You can check whether the interval estimate includes positive values, in which case you can't reject the H0 that the true variance is nonnegative:
>
> summary(fit, ci = TRUE)
>
>
> > 2) Will my sample size be an issue for publication, given that the are more parameters than observations (or units) in my model?
>
> Frankly, I think it should be.  To have any confidence in so many simultaneously estimated parameters, you need enough data to support it.  Using insufficient samples is one of the (many) root causes of the replicability crisis.  It is not just that your Type II error rate is high (low power), but when you make Type I errors, the estimated effect size must by definition be quite large to have been (incorrectly) flagged as significant.  Or even if there really is an effect, detecting it as significant will only happen when it is over estimated to a large degree, which makes it harder to trust even meta-analyses that accumulate information filtered by publication bias, etc.
>
> Is it possible to isolate particular hypotheses you want to test, that could be addressed with reduced models of a subset of variables at a time?  Sharing your syntax would help provide more well-informed advice.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject_clean: Covariances and Regressions don't match
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm really confused right now and can't figure out what I'm doing wrong. So I have a model like this:

model <- "
# bifactor
A =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + ... + x90
A1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 ...
A2 =~ x10 + x11 + x12 ...
A3 =~ x19 + x20 + x21 ...
...
A9 =~ ... + x88 + x89 + x90

# criteria
B =~ b1 + b2 + b3 + ... + b10
C =~ c1 + c2 + c3 + ... + c9
D =~ d1 + d2 + d3 + ... + d9
"
Bascially, A and B are two variables that are correlated pretty strongly. C and D are two variables that are expected to be related differently to A and B, so for example A~~C > B~~C and A~~D < B~~D. Thus, I fit the model (model.fit <- cfa(model, data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T)) and then check the correlations via inspect(model.fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>"). They are as follows:
A~~C = .130, B~~C = .185, A~~D = .580, B~~D = .744. So far so good.

Now I am also interested in the variance explained in C and D by A and B, respectively. So for each C and D, I estimate three seperate models: one with A, one with B and one with both A and B as predictors. I also let the specific factors of the bifactor model covary with the criterion. So for example, a regression model would look as follows:

reg.model <- "
# bifactor
A =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + ... + x90
A1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 ...
A2 =~ x10 + x11 + x12 ...
A3 =~ x19 + x20 + x21 ...
...
A9 =~ ... + x88 + x89 + x90

# criteria
B =~ b1 + b2 + b3 + ... + b10
C =~ c1 + c2 + c3 + ... + c9

# regression
C ~ A

# allowed covariances
C ~ B + A1 + A2 + A3 + ... + A9
"
Now, the betas look like this:
C ~ A beta = .293, R² = .079
C ~ B beta = .259, R² = .062

Shouldn't the correlation (i.e., the standardized covariance from the first model) and the beta be the same in the simple regression? And how is it possible, that the beta of C~B is smaller than the correlation C~~B?

I am really confused and hope somebody can shed a light here? Thanks so much in advance!

As soon as you have difference in residual covariances, Omega3 is more sensitive sensitive to these differences.

See in this example, that Omega3 is the one that presents bigger differences, specially when there is a resicual covariance present in one of the models, even in this case that the residual correlation is not large r = -.19

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

HS.model_rc <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

x2 ~~  x7
'

HS.model_vis <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3'

fit <- cfa(HS.model, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

summary(fit, standardized=T)

fit_rc <- cfa(HS.model_rc, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit_rc, standardized=T)

fit_vis <- cfa(HS.model_vis, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939)

round(cbind(reliability(fit)[,1],
            reliability(fit_rc)[,1],
            reliability(fit_vis)[,1]), 3)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am having some trouble getting the robust test statistic and associated fit indices (CFI, TLI, etc.) for a series of bivariate latent growth curve and random intercept cross-lagged panel models in a sparse (cohort-sequential) dataset with N=440 participants. For some of these models/variable combinations, lavaan returns NAs for these indices, and RMSEA point estimates & CIs are .00. There are no clear problems with the standard ML (not robust) statistics or convergence issues, so it seems to be specific to MLR.

I didn't have this problem when I ran the same models on the same data in the spring prior to updating to .6-7. I'm not certain whether I was using .6-6 or .6-5 at the time. The standard stats match up pretty well with what I got previously, but the robust stat issue is new. Was something changed in the update that would explain this problem, and what can I do to remedy it?

I found this github discussion <https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/95> that covers a similar issue, but from 2018 (so it would not be the same exact issue as mine), and the proposed solution (h1.information = "unstructured") does not help. Any help you can offer would be appreciated! Sample code for the bivariate LGCM below.

b.lgcm <- ' Intercept.X =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4 + 1*x5
          Linear.X =~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3 + 3*x4 + 4*x5
          Intercept.Y =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4 + 1*y5
          Linear.Y =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3 + 3*y4 + 4*y5 '
fit.lgcm <- growth(b.lgcm, data=data, missing = "FIML", estimator="MLR", em.iter.max = 20000)
summary(fit.lgcm, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the references, Dr. Jorgensen. Just to be clear, here is what I am doing: I want to test whether one variable’s regression coefficient, Z1, is invariant across two groups (Z4) in a structural model. In essence, I am attempting a moderation using multi-group analysis with SEM and categorical variables.
Here is the first model:
model.1 <- ‘
#measurement model
Y1 =~ X1 + X2 + X3 +X4 + X5
Y2 =~ X6 + X7 +X8
#structural model
Y1 ~ Y2 + Z1 + Z2 + Z3
Y2 ~ Z1 + Z2 + Z3’

fit_model.1 <-sem(model.1,
                                 data=mydata,
                                 group = “Z4”,
                                 ordered=c(“X1” , “X2” , “X3” , “X4” , “X5”,
                                  “X6” , “X7” , “X8” , “Z1” ,“Z2” , ”Z3”))

Per your previous response, I then constrain the regression coefficients for Z1 on Y1 to be equal across both groups in model 2, or:

Y1 ~ Y2 + c(b1, b1)* Z1 + Z2 + Z3

Here is the fit code for structural invariance model, constraining equality for thresholds, lv.covariances plus the one regression path for Z1 noted above:
fit_model.2 <-sem(model.2, data=mydata,
                                  group = “Z4”,
                                  group.equal=c(“thresholds”, "lv.covariances"),
                                  ordered=c(“X1” , “X2” , “X3” , “X4” ,+ “X5”,
                                                      “X6” , “X7” , “X8” , “Z1” ,“Z2” , ”Z3”))

 Now when I fit the model, the degrees of freedom are different; the chi-square test is not significant (p = 0.6745). No errors.

I conclude that the model is invariant with regard to the regression path for Z1 and there is no moderation concerning Z1. Does that look correct? (The Wu and Estabrook article was useful to understand the logic, but not the execution in Lavaan).

On Saturday, October 17, 2020 at 10:20:14 AM UTC-4 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > The p-value is not significant (p=0.333); therefore, I conclude the parameters are invariant across models
>
> Your test is invalid because you did not additionally constrain thresholds, so your latent item-response scales are not linked.  Including "intercepts" is meaningless with categorical indicators, unless you explicitly free some intercepts in the syntax, which is only identified if you constrain thresholds.  Read the Wu & Estabrook (2016) article <https://scholar.google.com/scholar_url?url=https://idp.springer.com/authorize/casa%3Fredirect_uri%3Dhttps://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0.pdf%26casa_token%3D3dYz0roxv80AAAAA:mUI9kO0ecfkFrl_IfYEcCzh1QXjQMKbI1JsdQpRg7cQmfiUo2aKlv2S_tsdlPOXhCL_k3OhBoQY9TA0WUg&hl=en&sa=T&oi=gsb-ggp&ct=res&cd=0&d=14667415196481628624&ei=VvyKX4_4IYqVmgGFtogQ&scisig=AAGBfm1YuNoqeAeHXn-YLv1zagMUvNmooA>.
>
>
> > I constrain only that parameter in the model: c(a,b)*x1
>
> You haven't provided your actual model syntax, so it is hard to tell what you are actually doing.  This is only the right-hand side of a parameter specification in lavaan model syntax, but I can tell it does not constrain the parameter to equality.  You labeled the parameter "a" in the first group and "b" in the second group, and you can verify in the summary() output whether the estimates are in fact unequal.  Giving the parameter the same label would constrain it to equality.
>
> https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html
>
>
> > My question is this: shouldn't the models be nested given I included the constraint for x1's slope in model.3?
>
> They might be nested, but the message says their df are the same, so if they are nested, they are equivalent.  You can verify this by printing each model and comparing their fit statistics.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm running a model with the MLMV estimator in Lavaan, and am now at the reporting stage. It is my understanding that it's good practice to report confidence intervals in addition to p-values, and so I do this for all hypotheses and also control variables. One of the control variables is gender, which is binary (coded as 0 or 1).

The p-value for gender is .048, and the confidence interval is (.00, 1.045). My question is: how should I interpret the upper limit here - can I safely state that this should be read as 1.0, or is this an indication that something is wrong? or should I simply report the values as reported by Lavaan?

I tried other estimators to double-check, but similar results.

thanks
klaas

have a just-significant effect of gender on js.

Pat

> If you specify in the cfa function that some/all items are categorical and estimator="wlsmv" (default with categorical items), them the estimated alpha dna omega will be calculated with the polychorical correlation matrix. The semTools function is smart enough to use the correct matrix depending of the type of item specified in cfa()
>
> Would only need to change this
>

> > > rels_fun <- function(obj){

messages.subject: adding moderator to multiple paths in a mediation
messages.subject_clean: adding moderator to multiple paths in a mediation
messages.body_plain:
Dear experts and community,

I am currently wanting to add a moderator to my mediation model. However, I have been told to add the moderator to all paths of the model (a, b, and c') to figure out at which point the moderator has an effect on the model. This seems to be possible in other packages such as PROCESS, but with Lavaan, it results in the 'duplicate model element' error, which makes sense as I am duplicating the effect of the moderator on both the b and c' paths (which have the same outcome, Y).

Is there a way to get around this in Lavaan, or should I test three separate models (with the moderator being on the a, b, and c' paths separately)? Alternatively, I can also specify models with the moderator on just the a and b paths, or a and c paths, but not sure if I can justify this, without having it also on the third path.

My syntax is as follows:
        # a path
         mediator ~ 1 + a1 * X
         mediator ~ a2 * moderator
         mediator ~ a3 * interaction (between X and moderator)

         # b paths
         Y ~ 1 + b1 * mediator
         Y ~ b2 * moderator
         Y ~ b3 * interaction (between mediator and moderator)

         # c prime path
         Y ~ 1 + cp * X
         Y ~ c2 * moderator
         Y ~ c3 * interaction (between X and moderator)

The highlighted text shows the duplicate - could I run the model after deleting one of the duplicates?

I apologise if these are naive questions as I do not have a strong statistical background - any help would be greatly appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: Difference between sem() and lavaan()
messages.subject_clean: Difference between sem() and lavaan()

The sem and cfa functions are wrappers for the sem function. This means, that some arguments have a certain default setting which are passed to the sem function: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lavaan/versions/0.6-7/topics/sem

"The sem function is a wrapper for the more general lavaan function, but setting the following default options: int.ov.free <http://int.ov.free> = TRUE, int.lv.free <http://int.lv.free> = FALSE, auto.fix.first <http://auto.fix.first> = TRUE (unless std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE), auto.fix.single <http://auto.fix.single> = TRUE, auto.var <http://auto.var> = TRUE, auto.cov.lv <http://auto.cov.lv>.x = TRUE, auto.efa <http://auto.efa> = TRUE, auto.th <http://auto.th> = TRUE, auto.delta <http://auto.delta> = TRUE, and auto.cov <http://auto.cov>.y = TRUE".

You can change all or individual default settings by passing your values to the sem function.

messages.body_plain:
> Does that look correct?

No, you cannot compare latent covariance-structure parameters without assuming metric invariance.  You need to constrain thresholds and loadings (but not necessarily intercepts) and test that against the configural model to see whether metric invariance is a tenable null hypothesis.  Then you can additionally constrain the latent regression slope to test that null hypothesis.  I have no idea why you would be constraining latent-variable covariances to equality.

messages.body_plain:
I see, thank you. I was cobbling together several tutorials so not sure myself (the categorical variables with thresholds is throwing me off--most examples for invariance testing use continuous data).

So following the standard test for invariance:
(1) configural
group = “Z4”,

(2) weak/metric
group = “Z4”,
group.equal=c("loadings")

(3) strong
group = “Z4”,
group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds")

(4) regression coefficients (if pervious invariance established)
group = “Z4”,
group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds", "regressions")

Or, use instead of "regressions" in group.equal, specify the one slope (Y1 ~ Y2 + c(b1, b1)* Z1 + Z2 + Z3)

On Wednesday, November 4, 2020 at 3:18:06 PM UTC-5 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > Does that look correct?
>
> No, you cannot compare latent covariance-structure parameters without assuming metric invariance.  You need to constrain thresholds and loadings (but not necessarily intercepts) and test that against the configural model to see whether metric invariance is a tenable null hypothesis.  Then you can additionally constrain the latent regression slope to test that null hypothesis.  I have no idea why you would be constraining latent-variable covariances to equality.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your replies - I think I'm now heading towards the right direction, and have edited my syntax according to Model 59:

         # a path
         M ~ 1 + a1 * X
         M ~ a2 * W
         M ~ a3 * XW

         # b path
         Y ~ 1 + b1 * M
         Y ~ b2 * MW

         # c prime path
         Y ~ c1 * X
         Y ~ c2 * W
         Y ~ c3 * XW

There is one more part I am not sure about, which is trying to get the indices of the indirect and direct effects. My moderator is binary (1 or 2) so I've specified the code as below:

         # index of moderated mediation and conditional indirect effects of XW on a path
         b1a3 := b1 * a3
         aELS1ss := a1 + a3 * 1 # simple slope for when moderator is 1
         aELS2ss := a1 + a3 * 2 # simple slope for when moderator is 2
         aELS1 := a1 * b1 + b1a3 * 1 # indirect effect
         aELS2 := a1 * b1 + b1a3 * 2

         # index of moderated mediation and conditional indirect effects of MW on b path
         a1b2 := a1 * b2
         bELS1ss := b1 + b2 * 1
         bELS2ss := b1 + b2 * 2
         bELS1 := a1 * b1 + a1b2 * 1 # indirect effect
         bELS2 := a1 * b1 + a1b2 * 2

         # index of moderated mediation and direct effects of XW on c path
         c1c3 := c1 * c3
         cELS1ss := c1 + c3 * 1
         cELS2ss := c1 + c3 * 2
         cELS1 := c1 + c1c3 * 1 # direct effect
         cELS2 := c1 + c1c3 * 2

It would be immensely helpful if anyone could let me know whether this is the correct way of specifying the effects. The syntax runs as is, so I'm not sure if I've specified everything as I should.

Thank you so much in advance.

messages.body_plain:
> what about alpha

semTools(reliability) and psych::alpha() should yield the same alpha for continuous data:

example(reliability) # alpha for the total (all 9 items) = 0.76
## all these also yield 0.76
alpha(HolzingerSwineford1939[paste0("x",1:9)])
alpha(cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[paste0("x",1:9)]))

If you are analyzing ordinal items, then semTools will calculate alpha from the polychoric correlations, whereas psych will treat them as continuous (as it says on the help page, as well as a message printed to the screen whenever running semTools::reliability() on ordinal data)

example(lavTables)
reliability(fit, return.total = TRUE)
## matches standard calculate on polychorics:
alpha(lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov)
## as opposed to treating binary data as numeric:
alpha(HSbinary)

You didn't provide the model syntax for the scalar model, so I can't see why it has fewer df than the partial-strict model.  But the script you did provide doesn't make sense.

You set parameterization = "theta" without declaring any variables as ordered=
If your indicators are ordinal (perhaps already of class c("ordered","factor") in the data.frame?), you cannot constrain intercepts or residuals without having constrained thresholds.  With free thresholds, the intercepts and residuals will be fixed, so they will be equal by default already.
You choose missing = "fiml", which is not available for ordinal outcomes.
You set group.partial = c("Exp =~ TA"), which is a loading, not a residual variance. Furthermore, it is the first loading, so fixed to 1 using ID.fac = "ul".  This would explain why no df were gained relative to the fully strict model.
You set ID.fac = "ul" yet effect.coding = "loadings", the latter of which would imply ID.fac = "fx"

> Question 1. Does the code look ok?

Except for group.equal = "configural", which doesn't make any sense.  It won't break anything, but "configural" is not a type of parameter.  For the configural model, you would just leave out the group.equal= argument because you aren't constraining any parameters.

> Question 2. If yes, how can chisquared be lower in models 3 & 4 compared to model 2?

You can't compare scaled/shifted chi-squared stats from different models.  The robust chi-squared difference test is calculated by scaling/shifting the difference between naive chi-squared stats from 2 nested models.  From your description, I can see you are gaining the correct number of degrees of freedom at each step, so I wouldn't worry about it.  To verify the models are nested, you could use the net() function.

Thanks a lot, Terence, for clarifying which things are wrong in the script.

You set parameterization = "theta" without declaring any variables as ordered=
If your indicators are ordinal (perhaps already of class c("ordered","factor") in the data.frame?), you cannot constrain intercepts or residuals without having constrained thresholds.  With free thresholds, the intercepts and residuals will be fixed, so they will be equal by default already.

In fact, I do not have ordinal data in the latent model, but numerical data (only the grouping variable gender is nominal). Therefore, I removed the command parameterization = "theta" now. If I understand it correctly, I do not need to define thresholds and do not need to check for threshold invariance when I have numeric data?

You choose missing = "fiml", which is not available for ordinal outcomes.

Since I have numeric and no ordinal variables, I keep missing = "fiml".

You set ID.fac = "ul" yet effect.coding = "loadings", the latter of which would imply ID.fac = "fx"

messages.body_plain:
> I came across this article that was very helpful, especially in explaining how thresholds figure into invariance testing: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/681607

I would be skeptical of the value of that tutorial.  It propagates the misunderstanding(s) that Wu & Estabrook (2016 <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5458787/>) have tried to clear up.  Namely, as I stated above: without equal thresholds, the latent item responses are not on linked scales, so loadings are not comparable.  The article you link to talks about simultaneously constraining thresholds and loadings (and intercepts, by virtue of not freeing them: another misunderstanding they propagate), which is fine, it just provides a single omnibus test of scalar invariance relative to configural invariance.  In comparison, they free loadings first, then thresholds, which is problematic for the reason in bold above.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I do not have ordinal data in the latent model, but numerical data (only the grouping variable gender is nominal). Therefore, I removed the command parameterization = "theta" now. If I understand it correctly, I do not need to define thresholds and do not need to check for threshold invariance when I have numeric data?

Correct.

> Indeed, I had first set ID.fac = "fx" to use the effect coding method. But then I got the warning message: "Higher-order factors detected. ID.fac set to "ul"."
> So I thought I would set ID.fac = "ul" intentionally and effect.coding = "loadings" as a separate command.

Why do you insist on using effects-coding for identification when the function told you that is not an option?  As the help page indicates:

> "In order to maintain generality, higher-order factors may include a mix of manifest and latent indicators, but they must therefore require ID.fac = "UL" to avoid complications with differentiating lower-order vs. higher-order (or mixed-level) factors."

> First question on this point: When testing the measurement invariance, is ID.fac = "fx" the only correct option

No, there is not even a good reason to prefer effects coding.  Contrary Little et al.'s (2006) <https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1301_3> boastful title, it is just as arbitrary as using a marker-variable or fixed-factor identification approach (e.g., you can constrain the loadings to average any number, not just 1).  Read a less biased comparison of the 3 approaches here:  https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1517356

Statistically equivalent parameterizations yield identical tests of (change in) fit, so if you want to use this function, use the identification method it requires and trust that you would get the same results if you wrote the syntax (with effects coding) yourself.

> can combine both commands?

No.

> is it still possible to use the effect coding method in a second-order model for the measurement invariance test? And if so, how?

Write the syntax yourself.  You can perhaps start by testing first-order invariance in CFA models without the higher-order factor, using measEq.syntax() to learn how to write the appropriate lavaan syntax.  Once you understand how to proceed, you can then copy the generated syntax adapt it by adding your higher-order factor and testing its parameters in whatever sequence you prefer.

>
> Maybe it is a very stupid question, but how do I modify the residual variance of individual indicators for testing the partial scalar measurement invariance?

Use the double-tilde operator to specify (co)variance parameters:   https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html

So to free the residual variances of items x1 and x5:

group.partial = c("x1~~x1","x5~~x5")

>  Also, in case I want to free a loading one time, and this would be the first loading, how would I do this? Is this generally not possible if ID.fac = "ul"?

You can't free a fixed loading without replacing it with another identification constraint.  This identification method has long been known as limited by its assumption that the reference indicator has no DIF.

>
> Or is it possible with ID.fac = "fx" instead?

The fixed-factor and effects-coding approaches both suffer from Type I error inflation because any test of a DIF-free item would be contaminated by invalid constraints on the item(s) that contain(s) DIF.  The better practice is to treat the free-one-item-at-a-time method as a way to identify a subset of anchor items that show the least evidence of DIF (i.e., smallest chi-squared stats).  Then, only apply constraints on those anchor items, and test remaining items for DIF by constraining (rather than freeing) one item at a time.  Find a description in Woods (2009) <https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0146621607314044>.

Again, if you are testing first-order loadings for DIF, you can do this in a CFA without the higher-order factor to use either fixed-factor or effects-coding identification.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

as it is supposed to be the reference group, I went with the next suggestion
which was baseline group at FU2 for ‘bullied’. This parameter was freely
estimated in the baseline model, so it seemed OK to free it here.

I tried different combinations of
measEq.syntax to free this parameter but it always seemed to either only free
the female group or both males and females, so I decided to write the syntax
myself so that it only frees the male group at FU2.

Is there a way to do this in
measEq.syntax that I was missing? If not, is there a reason why I shouldn’t
free this parameter? The syntax that I wrote works, but I wanted to check
whether there would be a reason not to do this. I have been having problems
with models I have been running that have been using these measurement
invariance constraints, so I am trying to determine whether the problem lies
here.

Jess

BL.popular ~~ c(NA, NA)*FU2.popular + c(theta.8_3.g1, theta.8_3.g2)*FU2.popular

BL.bullied ~~ c(NA, NA)*FU2.bullied + c(theta.9_4.g1, theta.9_4.g2)*FU2.bullied

BL.oldbest ~~ c(NA, NA)*FU2.oldbest + c(theta.10_5.g1, theta.10_5.g2)*FU2.oldbest

## LATENT MEANS/INTERCEPTS:

BL.PP ~ c(0, NA)*1 + c(alpha.1.g1, alpha.1.g2)*1

FU2.PP ~ c(NA, NA)*1 + c(alpha.2.g1, alpha.2.g2)*1

## COMMON-FACTOR VARIANCES:

BL.PP ~~ c(1, NA)*BL.PP + c(psi.1_1.g1, psi.1_1.g2)*BL.PP

FU2.PP ~~ c(NA, NA)*FU2.PP + c(psi.2_2.g1, psi.2_2.g2)*FU2.PP

## COMMON-FACTOR COVARIANCES:

BL.PP ~~ c(NA, NA)*FU2.PP + c(psi.2_1.g1, psi.2_1.g2)*FU2.PP'

PP.intercepts5 <- cfa(PP.intercepts5.syntax, data = outlong_data,

On Tuesday, November 10, 2020 at 8:18:28 PM UTC Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > I do not have ordinal data in the latent model, but numerical data (only the grouping variable gender is nominal). Therefore, I removed the command parameterization = "theta" now. If I understand it correctly, I do not need to define thresholds and do not need to check for threshold invariance when I have numeric data?
>
> Correct.
>
> > Indeed, I had first set ID.fac = "fx" to use the effect coding method. But then I got the warning message: "Higher-order factors detected. ID.fac set to "ul"."
> > So I thought I would set ID.fac = "ul" intentionally and effect.coding = "loadings" as a separate command.
>
> Why do you insist on using effects-coding for identification when the function told you that is not an option?  As the help page indicates:
>
> > "In order to maintain generality, higher-order factors may include a mix of manifest and latent indicators, but they must therefore require ID.fac = "UL" to avoid complications with differentiating lower-order vs. higher-order (or mixed-level) factors."
>
> > First question on this point: When testing the measurement invariance, is ID.fac = "fx" the only correct option
>
> No, there is not even a good reason to prefer effects coding.  Contrary Little et al.'s (2006) <https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1301_3> boastful title, it is just as arbitrary as using a marker-variable or fixed-factor identification approach (e.g., you can constrain the loadings to average any number, not just 1).  Read a less biased comparison of the 3 approaches here:  https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1517356
>
> Statistically equivalent parameterizations yield identical tests of (change in) fit, so if you want to use this function, use the identification method it requires and trust that you would get the same results if you wrote the syntax (with effects coding) yourself.
>
>
> > can combine both commands?
>
> No.
>
> > is it still possible to use the effect coding method in a second-order model for the measurement invariance test? And if so, how?
>
> Write the syntax yourself.  You can perhaps start by testing first-order invariance in CFA models without the higher-order factor, using measEq.syntax() to learn how to write the appropriate lavaan syntax.  Once you understand how to proceed, you can then copy the generated syntax adapt it by adding your higher-order factor and testing its parameters in whatever sequence you prefer.
>
> >
> > Maybe it is a very stupid question, but how do I modify the residual variance of individual indicators for testing the partial scalar measurement invariance?
>
> Use the double-tilde operator to specify (co)variance parameters:   https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html
>
> So to free the residual variances of items x1 and x5:
>
> group.partial = c("x1~~x1","x5~~x5")
>
>
> >  Also, in case I want to free a loading one time, and this would be the first loading, how would I do this? Is this generally not possible if ID.fac = "ul"?
>
> You can't free a fixed loading without replacing it with another identification constraint.  This identification method has long been known as limited by its assumption that the reference indicator has no DIF.
>
> >
> > Or is it possible with ID.fac = "fx" instead?
>
> The fixed-factor and effects-coding approaches both suffer from Type I error inflation because any test of a DIF-free item would be contaminated by invalid constraints on the item(s) that contain(s) DIF.  The better practice is to treat the free-one-item-at-a-time method as a way to identify a subset of anchor items that show the least evidence of DIF (i.e., smallest chi-squared stats).  Then, only apply constraints on those anchor items, and test remaining items for DIF by constraining (rather than freeing) one item at a time.  Find a description in Woods (2009) <https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0146621607314044>.
>
> Again, if you are testing first-order loadings for DIF, you can do this in a CFA without the higher-order factor to use either fixed-factor or effects-coding identification.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

That's a pretty cool name to have in the age of the Star Wars sequel trilogy :-)

> Does anyone know what I may be missing?

The moderation syntax looks fine.  Does your output not match?

The mediation output indicates that ReunificationwithParent is a binary output (one threshold), so you need to tell lavaan that:

fit <- sem(model, ordered="ReunificationwithParent", data = Mediation)

And you cannot currently request a logit link unless you use estimator = "MML"; otherwise, the default is the probit link (see the ?lavOpstions help page).  But that should match your matlab output, which has a threshold estimate (I assume that implies you are relying on the latent-response interpretation of the probit model, although strictly speaking the logistiic model also has that interpretation).

Also, your matlab output does not indicate to what value the residual variance of ReunificationwithParent is fixed in order to identify the model, but the default in lavaan is the same as in Mplus: parameterization = "delta" implies the marginal variance of the latent response underlying ReunificationwithParent == 1.  If your matlab code is doing the standard approach for probit models (i.e., the linear predictor is transformed to a cumulative standard-normal probability), then that is consistent with the conditional / residual variance being fixed to 1 using the argument parameterization = "theta".

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

>  group.partial = "FU2.popular ~ c(0, NA)*1"

group.partial= only accepts a parameter, so this should be simply:

group.partial = "FU2.popular ~ 1"

as you specify for long.partial=.  I assume long.partial = "popular ~ 1" worked fine?

You can also use the update() method, which has a change.syntax= argument you can use to pass any changes you want to make.  If you didn't overwrite the PP.intercepts.syntax object with your as.character() conversion, you could do this:

PP.intercepts2.syntax <- update(PP.intercepts.syntax,
                                change.syntax = c("FU2.popular ~ c(0, NA)*1",
                                                  "FU2.oldbest ~ c(0, NA)*1"))

That's why in the help page examples, I give the character string a different stem, like mod.x <- as.character(syntax.x)

See the class?measEq.syntax help page, and an example on GitHub:  https://github.com/simsem/semTools/issues/60

messages.body_plain:
>  - Also, Is there a consensus between MLR and WLSMV estimators?

5 or more categories can typically be treated as continuous with MLR, unless there are very few responses in tail categories (e.g., as a result of asymmetric thresholds), in which case 7 categories are preferred before treating as continuous:

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

> > - Am I doing right?
> >
> > - Are the calls in cfa() correct (sintaxe/code)?

Looks fine, except you don't need the argument orthogonal=FALSE because that is the default for cfa()
Likewise, when you declare outcomes as ordered=, the default is estimator = "WLSMV", so no need for that.
But it doesn't hurt to explicitly state either argument.

> > - In fitmeasures(m0_cfa), which is the print above, all what I need to look at are on the right-most measures (under “Robust” column), when there are two columns. One curious thing is that the “robust” estimators of #Aproach 2 are available under the name of “scaled”, not “robust” when I call summary(m0_cfa, fit.measures = T)

the ones explicitly labeled "robust" are consistent estimators of their population counterparts, so they are preferred to the "scaled" versions, which simply apply the normal-theory formulas to robust chi-squared statistics.

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2018.1455142

> >
> > - So, how should I report the CFI indicator? (as "scaled" or "robust"?).

When "robust" is available (with MLR), report it and cite the papers that proposed them:

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2012.715252

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2014.933697

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
One of my latent variables is formed by 4 indicators, 2 of them are negatively worded therefore I reversed the scores. From an EFA the 2 reversed items form a distinct factor, I tried to keep them anyway but the CFA and then the SEM confirmed several problems in the model due to those two items (an inspection of the residual matrix confirmed me that).

So I dropped the two reversed items (I won't use reversed items never again in my life!)

The model works with two items that form the latent factor, but I know that a latent variable with only two indicators is not appropriate (unless any exceptions?).

I think the solution would be to use an aggregated measure of the two items, using the variable as observed, and constraining the error variance as suggested by Bollen (1989).

All this long story to ask you if the constraining should be specified as follow:

var ~~#*var
​
(where "#" is 1 - reliability). Is it correct?

When doing that, the model fit is not good anymore. Since the reliability I took from previous study does not reflect the exact same construct (items were a bit different in the meaning, and I did not found anything else closer), would be acceptable to keep the two items (var=~ item1 + item2)? I know this last question is not about Lavaan syntax but I would really appreciate your thoughts .

Thank you very much,

Fran

messages.body_plain:
Fran,

There are two main reasons to be concerned about only two items per factor.

The big one is identification. Generally speaking, a latent needs
three outgoing paths to be identified in the absence of additional
constraints. These can be to three or more indicators, or to two
indicators and an endogenous variable at the structural level.* In a
CFA, there is no structural level, so that's where the minimum of
three indicators comes from. Another possibility is additional
constraints. if your two items are from a scale and have comparable
metrics, it may be appropriate to constrain the two loadings to
equality.

The other big concern is that in a common-factor theory, you are
generally assuming that your indicators are representative of the
domain theoretically being measured. Depending on the domain and the
nature of the indicators, that may imply you want more. A small number
of homogenous items is measuring something relatively specific (which
may be what you want).

*You may have noticed the implication that the endogenous variable is
functioning much like an indicator. This is, in a sense, true,
especially if the structural relation is strong. This can be another
reason to have more indicators, to dilute this effect.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: "Guide"/Final considerations/recomendations on CFA for ordinal response variables
messages.subject_clean: "Guide"/Final considerations/recomendations on CFA for ordinal response variables
messages.body_plain:
If those variables are treated as ordinal, then their latent-response's residual variances are not estimable (at least, not without constraints on the thresholds).  By default (parameterization="delta"), the latent-response scales (~*~) are fixed to 1, and residual variances are merely implied as 1 minus the explained variance.

But if this is happening when you treat those variables as continuous, then something else is going on.  In which case a minimal script (and maybe some data) would be required to see what is happening.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
> Am I doing this right?
Looks right.
> How do I interpret the output?
https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html
Try Googling for more tutorials about growth curves in lavaan, like this one: https://quantdev.ssri.psu.edu/tutorials/growth-modeling-chapter-10-growth-models-nonlinearity-time

> Why are all intercepts 0?
They aren't.  Only the indicators have intercepts == 0 because their means are reproduces as functions of the growth parameters.  The growth parameter means are merely very close to zero (try adding the argument nd=7 for the summary() to print up to 7 digits of precision).  Slopes nearly zero seems very consistent with the dark blue line in your plot being almost flat.  The plot indicates your (unconditional) average intercept should be somewhere between 2 and 3; however,  you have several predictors of the growth factors.  Thus, the intercepts are the mean level and change when all those predictors == 0.  Does that make sense for your data?
> What does it mean that intercept, slope, and quadratic slope are not significant?
It implies those parameters are consistent with a population parameter == 0.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Error in colSums(S) : 'x' must be an array of at least two dimensions

The code I am using in lavaan is below:

m0 = '
WM =~ NA*BSS3 + NA*FSS3 + NA*LTRS3 + NA*SPRS3
AC =~ NA*SSUS3 + NA*SIMP3 + NA*TNT3
IR =~ NA*STRP3 + NA*FLNK3 + NA*TKSW3 + NA*BOX3

# (Co)variances
WM ~~ a*IR
WM ~~ 1*AC
IR ~~ a*AC
WM ~~ 1*WM
AC ~~ 1*AC
IR ~~ 1*IR
BSS3 ~~ BSS3
FSS3 ~~ FSS3
LTRS3 ~~ LTRS3
SPRS3 ~~ SPRS3
SSUS3 ~~ SSUS3
SIMP3 ~~ SIMP3
TNT3 ~~ TNT3
FLNK3 ~~ FLNK3
STRP3 ~~ STRP3
TKSW3 ~~ TKSW3
BOX3 ~~ BOX3

# Intercepts
WM ~ 0*1
IR ~ 0*1
AC ~ 0*1
BSS3 ~ 1
FSS3 ~ 1
LTRS3 ~ 1
SPRS3 ~ 1
SSUS3 ~ 1
SIMP3 ~ 1
TNT3 ~ 1
FLNK3 ~ 1
STRP3 ~ 1
TKSW3 ~ 1
BOX3 ~ 1
'

m1 = '
WM =~ NA*BSS3 + NA*FSS3 + NA*LTRS3 + NA*SPRS3
AC =~ NA*SSUS3 + NA*SIMP3 + NA*TNT3
IR =~ NA*STRP3 + NA*FLNK3 + NA*TKSW3 + NA*BOX3

# (Co)variances
WM ~~ IR
WM ~~ AC
IR ~~ AC
WM ~~ 1*WM
AC ~~ 1*AC
IR ~~ 1*IR
BSS3 ~~ BSS3

LTRS3 ~~ LTRS3
SPRS3 ~~ SPRS3

# Intercepts

Hi
There are some problems with me in your model:
1- you clarify your dependent variables as ordered, do you think they are ordinal variables? If so, no problem.
2- In your theoretical model all indicators related to demographic variables (and other independent variables) are not present, while in your command you insert all of them for all dependent variables. if this happened just for summary, no problem.

as i told before you have checked a saturated model, so your df is 0 and your fit indices are in maximum. of course no evaluation you can do with saturated models.
just check if your dependent variables are ordinal or not. otherwise you run your path analysis correctly. HTH

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am conducting a measurement invariance analysis across three groups using the measEq.syntax function and following Wu & Estabrook guidelines. I started with the configural model, then constrained thresholds, and then loadings. It appears the measure's structure, threshold, and loadings are invariant, so now I'd like to constrain means to assess if latent means differ between groups. When I use the measEq.syntax, there is no difference in my loading invariance model and my mean invariance model (exact same fit and df) and I get the following warning message:

In measEq.syntax(configural.model = EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC, data = menEDE,  :  Latent means are not comparable across groups if their respective factor loadings and intercepts are not equal across groups.

I am able to accomplish this if I don't use measEq.syntax() and instead just use the cfa() function. That is, model fit and df are different in the means invariance model using just cfa() and not measEq.syntax(). But, I know I'm doing something wrong if it's not working with measEq.syntax() so I don't want to abandon ship and proceed in my ignorance.

Below is my model and syntax. I wanted to freely estimate all loadings and not have a referent indicator, for context. I didn't want to assume invariance of any loadings.

#model

EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC <- 'BodyDisL =~ NA*ede32 + ede33

OverValL =~ NA*ede29 + ede30

ResL =~ NA*ede1 + ede3 + ede4

BodyDisL ~~ OverValL + ResL

OverValL ~~ ResL

BodyDisL ~~ 1*BodyDisL

OverValL ~~ 1*OverValL

ResL ~~ 1*ResL'

#configural invariance

baseline<-measEq.syntax(configural.model=EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC, ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", parameterization = "theta", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "racecat", group.equal = "configural", ordered = c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

model.baseline<-as.character(baseline)

fit.baseline<-cfa(model.baseline, data=menEDE, group="racecat", ordered = c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

summary(fit.baseline)

#threshold invariance

prop4<-measEq.syntax(configural.model = EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC, data = menEDE, group="racecat", group.equal="thresholds", parameterization="delta", ID.fac="std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu.Estabrook.2016", ordered=c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

model.prop4<-as.character(prop4)

fit.prop4<-cfa(model.prop4, data=menEDE, group="racecat", ordered = c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

summary(fit.prop4, fit.measures=T)

#loadings invariance

 EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC, data = menEDE, group="racecat", group.equal=c("thresholds", "loadings"), parameterization="delta", ID.fac="std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu.Estabrook.2016", ordered=c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

model.prop7<-as.character(prop7)

fit.prop7<-cfa(model.prop7, data=menEDE, group="racecat", ordered = c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

summary(fit.prop7, fit.measures=T)

#mean invariance

means<-measEq.syntax(configural.model = EDEQ.allmodelmod3FAC, data = menEDE, group="racecat", group.equal=c("thresholds", "loadings", "means"), parameterization="delta", ID.fac="std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu.Estabrook.2016", ordered=c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

model.means<-as.character(means)

fit.means<-cfa(model.means, data=menEDE, group="racecat", ordered = c("ede1", "ede3", "ede4", "ede29", "ede30", "ede32", "ede33"))

summary(fit.prop7, fit.measures=T)

messages.subject: Re: Fixing Error variance with ordered categorical data
messages.subject_clean: Fixing Error variance with ordered categorical data
messages.body_plain:
> in lavaan WLSMV estimator by default use the delta parameterization method, and I believe that this method does not allow setting a negative error variance to a value close to zero

Correct, error variances are not model parameters under delta parameterization.  They are merely implied by the latent scales and the explained variance.

> My question is: how can I estimate in lavaan a model using the WLSMV estimator with  theta parameterization?

If your error variance is negative under delta, I would guess your model would fail to converge under theta parameterization, because that variance would be fixed to 1 for identification.

The issue is not the negative variance; that is just one side of a two-sided coin.  The explained variance exceeds 1, which is what the delta parameterization assumes the total variance is.  Fixing that variance to zero would not solve the "problem" anyway, only mask it, and in so doing, create other problems.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

If you only have 1 predictor, all explained variance is due to a single parameter, so you could check the CI around its standardized value to test whether its population value < 1 (which would imply the population error variance > 0).

https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0049124112442138

For example, if this is an indicator in a CFA, you could use std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE to fix factor variances to 1, in which case loadings under the delta parameterization are already standardized parameters.  So you could request summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Does TYPE IS MISSING return summary statistics and proportions of missing data per variable?  I don't see that TYPE option listed in their manual:

Perhaps it only deleted missing cases per variable, rather than cases that have missing values on any variable in USEVARIABLES (which you did not specify).  Difficult to tell without attaching the Mplus output file.

messages.body_plain:
> Latent means are not comparable across groups if their respective factor loadings and intercepts are not equal across groups.

As the message says, you need to additionally constrain intercepts in order for latent means to be comparable.  If intercepts are not constrained, then latent means are simply fixed to zero for identification.  So add 1 more step (scalar invariance): group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts").
If scalar invariance does not significantly deteriorate fit relative to metric invariance, you can then compare scalar invariance to group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts","means")

messages.body_plain:
Terence. Thanks for the clarifications, they will be of great use to me.
 Best regards

> El 14 nov 2020, a las 22:41, Terrence Jorgensen <TJorge...@GMAIL.COM> escribió:
>

> > in lavaan WLSMV estimator by default use the delta parameterization method, and I believe that this method does not allow setting a negative error variance to a value close to zero
>
> Correct, error variances are not model parameters under delta parameterization.  They are merely implied by the latent scales and the explained variance.
>
> > My question is: how can I estimate in lavaan a model using the WLSMV estimator with  theta parameterization?
>
> If your error variance is negative under delta, I would guess your model would fail to converge under theta parameterization, because that variance would be fixed to 1 for identification.
>
> The issue is not the negative variance; that is just one side of a two-sided coin.  The explained variance exceeds 1, which is what the delta parameterization assumes the total variance is.  Fixing that variance to zero would not solve the "problem" anyway, only mask it, and in so doing, create other problems.
>
> https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150
>
> If you only have 1 predictor, all explained variance is due to a single parameter, so you could check the CI around its standardized value to test whether its population value < 1 (which would imply the population error variance > 0).
>
> https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0049124112442138
>
> For example, if this is an indicator in a CFA, you could use std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE to fix factor variances to 1, in which case loadings under the delta parameterization are already standardized parameters.  So you could request summary(fit, ci = TRUE)
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>
>

not.

messages.body_plain:
> How to perform simulations for a Likert scale order data 5 for a multi-group model?

See the ?simulateData help page for a single-group example and normal data.  I adapted that example below (using just 1 factor, so a CFA with 3 indicators) in two ways:
to make it for multiple groups by supplying vectors of parameters (1 per group) and passing a vector of sample sizes to the sample.nobs= argument
I added 4 thresholds for variables x1-x3 to make them categorical.
That shows you the basic functionality, and you can generalize from there to your own goals.

population.model <- ' f1 =~ c(.7, .7)*x1 + c(0.8, 0.8)*x2 + c(0.7, 0.8)*x3
## factor variance
  f1 ~~ c(1, 1)*f1
## residual variances (such that indicator total variances == 1)
  x1 ~~ c(.51, .51)*x1
  x2 ~~ c(.36, .36)*x2
  x3 ~~ c(.51, .36)*x3
## thresholds
  x1 | -1.5*t1 + -0.5*t2 + 0.5*t3 + 1.5*t4
  x2 | -2*t1 + -1*t2 + 0*t3 + 1*t4
  x3 | -1*t1 + 0*t2 + 1*t3 + 2*t4
'
## generate data
set.seed(1234)
myData <- simulateData(population.model, sample.nobs = c(100L, 100L),
                       parameterization = "theta")
## quick check
opar <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1))
for (i in 1:3) hist(myData[ , paste0("x", i)])
par(opar)

messages.body_plain:
> Therefore, correct testing is not possible.

well, testing is not possible period with df=0

> R showed, that there were definetly more than 0 degrees of freedom. Now I'm a bit confused.

Only a first-order CFA with 3 variables has df=0.  With multiple factors, you have df>0 because there are fewer factor correlations than correlations between indicators of different factors.

However, your second-order factor is just-identified and lonely, so that model is statistically equivalent to a first-order CFA without the higher-order factor.  So you still can't test the H0 of a second-order factor structure, unless you make a bolder claim, such as tau-equivalence (equal loadings) or parallel items (equal loadings & residual variances), or ...

> Actually I wanted to use this model (one second-order factor, three first-order factors, each with three indicators) and test it for invariance. But I am not sure, whether this is appropriate from a statistical point of view or not.

Yes,  invariance of second-order measurement parameters is still testable because it places more than minimal identification constraints,

Wow. It really was that simple! Thank you so much. Constraining the intercepts did the trick. There was indeed scalar invariance and then I was able to also constrain means. Thank you so much for your prompt and helpful reply!

On Sat, Nov 14, 2020 at 4:59 PM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Latent means are not comparable across groups if their respective factor loadings and intercepts are not equal across groups.
> As the message says, you need to additionally constrain intercepts in order for latent means to be comparable.  If intercepts are not constrained, then latent means are simply fixed to zero for identification.  So add 1 more step (scalar invariance): group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts").
> If scalar invariance does not significantly deteriorate fit relative to metric invariance, you can then compare scalar invariance to group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts","means")
>

messages.body_plain:
> model <- '
> factor1 =~ x1+x2+x3
> factor2 =~ x4+x5+x6
> factor3 =~ x7+x8+x9
> higherorderfactor =~ factor1+factor2+factor3'
>
> This model is just-identified. Therefore, I need to make constraints, for example same factor loadings:

No, there are plenty of degrees of freedom.  As I explained in my previous post, this model is statistically equivalent to a first-order CFA model:

model <- '
factor1 =~ x1+x2+x3
factor2 =~ x4+x5+x6

factor3 =~ x7+x8+x9 '

And you don't need to make arbitrary constraints unless they represent actual hypotheses you want to test.  Tau-equivalence and parallel indicators were examples, not instructions, and I was only referring to the higher-order factor's loadings and residual variances, not the first-order measurement model (whose fit is already testable).

> If someone has reliable information (i.e. articles) on invariance testing for second-order models, I would be grateful if you could post it.

Here are 2 tutorials with different approaches (both valid):

http://dx.doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1302_7

https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1203_7

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

cfa_esp <- '# Definição das Variáveis latentes (CFA)

             AnáliseDaMissão =~ TEA1 + TEA2 + TEA3 + TEA4 + TEA5
             EspecificaçãoDasMetas =~ TEB1 + TEB2 + TEB3 + TEB4  + TEB5 + TEB6
             Planejamento =~ TEC1 + TEC2 + TEC3 + TEC4  + TEC5 + TEC6

             PREPARAÇÃO =~ AnáliseDaMissão + EspecificaçãoDasMetas + Planejamento

             # EXECUÇÃO
             Coordenação =~ TED1 + TED2 + TED3 + TED4
             Cooperação =~ TEE1 + TEE2 + TEE3 + TEE4
             Comunicação =~ TEF1 + TEF2 + TEF3 + TEF4

             EXECUÇÃO =~ Coordenação + Cooperação + Comunicação

             # AVALIAÇÃO
             MonitoramentoDoDesempenho =~ TEG1 + TEG2 + TEG3 + TEG4  + TEG5 + TEG6
             MonitoramentoDeSistemas =~ TEH1 + TEH2 + TEH3 + TEH4

             AVALIAÇÃO =~ MonitoramentoDoDesempenho + MonitoramentoDeSistemas

             # AJUSTES
             ResoluçãoDeProblemas =~ TEI1 + TEI2 + TEI3 + TEI4
             Inovação =~ TEJ1 + TEJ2 + TEJ3 + TEJ4
             TreinamentoInterno =~ TEK1 + TEK2 + TEK3 + TEK4
             PrestarSuporte =~ TEL1 + TEL2 + TEL3 + TEL4 + TEL5

             AJUSTES =~ ResoluçãoDeProblemas + Inovação + TreinamentoInterno + PrestarSuporte

             # GME
             GestãoIntegrativaDeConflitos =~ TEM1 + TEM2 + TEM3 + TEM4
             SuportePsicológico =~ TEN1 + TEN2 + TEN3 + TEN4

             GME =~ GestãoIntegrativaDeConflitos + SuportePsicológico
           '
I run:
m0_cfa <- cfa(cfa_esp, data =data, orthogonal = F, estimator = "MLR")
and I see from fitmeasures(), cronbach alpha, etc... that my model is great.

However, I also want to test whether every smaller model, such as:
             # PREPARAÇÃO
             AnáliseDaMissão =~ TEA1 + TEA2 + TEA3 + TEA4 + TEA5
             EspecificaçãoDasMetas =~ TEB1 + TEB2 + TEB3 + TEB4  + TEB5 + TEB6

Or, because the bigger model is suitable, is it no longer necessary?

I ask this because I may want to use PREPARACAO separate from other constructs.

Thanks in advance!!

> Or, because the bigger model is suitable, is it no longer necessary?

That is my opinion.  Individual CFAs per construct might provide some information about lack of fit among those indicators, but they would not tell you anything about misfit due to your model failing to reproduce relationships between indicators of different constructs.  So if you had evidence against your full model being a good fit, (i.e., significant chi-squared) you would want to investigate why using (e.g.) correlation residuals from the full model.

'

messages.subject_clean: modelfit worse through contraining intercepts z-standardized variables
messages.body_plain:
> I am fitting a model with several z-standardized variables.

Don't do that, unless you understand how to constrain residual variances such that the model-implied total variances == 1 (which is fixed for correlations).  Otherwise, you will have inflated Type I error rates.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.105.2.317

> I thought that constraining their intercepts to zero would necessarily improve my model fit. This is not the case and I was wondering if anyone knows why.

The sample means of z-scores calculated using sample M & SD are 0 by definition.  But means are not model parameters.  Intercepts are expected values (means) of the outcome when its predictor(s) equal(s) zero.  Not sure what your model looks like, but if it is just a CFA with latent mean(s) fixed to zero, then it would make sense for indicator intercepts to also be zero (within the bounds of machine precision, so zero to 15 digits or so) because the expected value of an outcome is its grand mean when holding all predictors at their grand means.  But with more complicated models, that would not necessarily be the case.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
I love the lavaan package. Thank you Yves, Terrence, and others for developing it.

I was wondering whether you have interest/plans to extend lavaaan to allow moderated nonlinear factor analysis? This would be particularly helpful for testing measurement invariance across many different factors simultaneously, including continuous factors. The regularization approach proposed by Bauer et al. (2020) seems to be a promising approach for testing for measurement invariance across multiple factors.

Bauer, D. J., Belzak, W. C. M., & Cole, V. T. (2020). Simplifying the assessment of measurement invariance over multiple background variables: Using regularized moderated nonlinear factor analysis to detect differential item functioning. Structural Equation Modeling, 27(1), 43–55. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1642754

Bauer, D. J. (2017). A more general model for testing measurement invariance and differential item functioning. Psychological Methods, 22(3), 507–526. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000077

On Monday, September 7, 2020 at 5:15:01 AM UTC-5 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I  am wondering if such a  MIMIC model plus a moderated factor loading could  be estimated in lavaan as well
>
> MNLFA is not MIMIC.  In MIMIC, variables are regressed on other variables.  In MNLFA, parameters are regressed on other variables (the latter of which are not even "modeled" variables).  This is a more general case of something like Mplus's TSCORES which allow a different (fixed) Lambda matrix per case in a latent curve model.
>
> lavaan does not allow for this.  The parameters must be considered constant across cases (within each group in a multigroup model).
>
> It is possible in OpenMx.  See work by Dylan Molenaar on heteroskedastic latent trait models, which I think could be considered a special case of MNLFA.  My grad student is working on a tutorial article on MNLFA in OpenMx; I'll try to remember to post a link here once a preprint is available.
>
> > not sure if Lavaan  offers something similar to the  MODEL CONSTRAINT' command)?
>
> Yes, but it only accommodates functions of (estimated) parameters.  Adapted from the ?lavTestWald help page:
>
> HS.model <- '
>   visual =~ x1 + b1*x2 + x3
>   textual =~ x4 + b2*x5 + x6

messages.subject: Issues related to output of latent growth model with covariates
messages.subject_clean: Issues related to output of latent growth model with covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Professors,

I have several questions related to the output of latent growth model with covariates.

For example, I fit a linear latent growth model with 4 time points' panel data, and here is the code I used in lavaan:

# i means latent intercept and s means the latent slope
i=~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
s=~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3+ 3*x4

# latent growth model with covariates
i~cov1+cov2
s~cov1+cov2

>From this latent growth model, I could get the mean of i and s, and the estimates of i and s regressing on cov1 and cov2 from the summary of the fit model. My questions are:

(1) If I would like to get the estimated mean of i and s for the whole population with covariates, is it calculated like this?
 Estimated Intercept Mean =
                                                  Estimated Intercept +
                                                  Estimated Slope (cov1)* Sample Mean (cov1) +
                                                  Estimated Slope (cov2)* Sample Mean (cov2)
If this formula is correct,  it must be calculated by hand? or I could use some functions in lavaan? I have used Lavpredict before, but I think it could give i and s for each observation, but could not give the estimated mean of whole population.

(2) When I calculated the Estimated intercept mean for the whole population from the question (1), how can I determine whether it deviates from some values, for example, mean slope deviating from 0?

(3) If I could use the formula in question (1), how to set the mean value for cov1 and cov2 if they are categorical variables?

Thank you very much.

Regards

Xueying

messages.subject: Re: Issues related to output of latent growth model with covariates
messages.subject_clean: Issues related to output of latent growth model with covariates
messages.body_plain:
Xueying

If you mean-center cov1 and cov2 before analysis (e.g., with scale() ), questions 1 and 2 take care of themselves. The model-implied means of i and s become the estimated intercepts of i and s, and by default they are tested against zero in the output.

However, question 3 puts a wrench in things. There is no such thing as the mean of a categorical variable. If the variables are nominal, you could effect-code and then mean-center the effect codes.

Pat

messages.subject: How to interpret standardized coefficients for latent variable in CFA?
messages.subject_clean: How to interpret standardized coefficients for latent variable in CFA?
messages.body_plain:
Hello there!

I am fitting a CFA model with the following syntax:

    cfa_esp <- ' Tarefa =~ Coop. + Esf.Melh. + PapelImp.
                 Ego =~ Pun.Erros + Recon.Desig. + Riv.Membr.'
    m0_cfa <- cfa(cfa_esp, data =data, orthogonal = F, estimator = "WLSMV")

And I obtain these results from the coefficients:

    summary(m0_cfa, standardized = T)$PE

    Latent Variables:
                             Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
      Tarefa =~
        Coop.                   1.000                               0.688    0.891
        Esf.Melh.               0.639    0.042   15.170    0.000    0.439    0.793
        PapelImp.               0.677    0.043   15.678    0.000    0.466    0.797
      Ego =~
        Pun.Erros               1.000                               0.262    0.403
        Recon.Desig.            4.872    1.514    3.218    0.001    1.277    1.388
        Riv.Membr.              1.069    0.221    4.834    0.000    0.280    0.307

How can I interpret `Std.all` column?

This is my try for each estimate column:

+ A unit increase in `Tarefa` implies in .639 units increase in `Esf.Melh.`;
+ One standard deviation increase in `Tarefa` implies in .439 units increase in `Esf.Melh.`
+ The correlation of `PapelImp.` and `Tarefa` is .797 (since we are building latent variable, Std.all is interpreted as correlation);

This is what I thought it was right. However, the Std.all coefficient is 1.388 for `Ego` and `Recon.Desig.`. So, how can I interpret these coefficients?

Thanks
Obs.: I also made this question on stats.stackexchange <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/497171/how-to-interpret-standardized-coefficients-for-latent-variable-in-cfa>. Thanks

messages.body_plain:
A standardized loading over 1 is an impermissible solution, but judging the large standard error on the unstandardized coefficient it may not be significantly over 1.

That said, the standardized loadings on Ego are widely disparate, especially with only three items. You may have an empirical underidentification issue. I would go back and examine the (polychoric?) correlation matrix, as well as the residual correlation matrix from the CFA.

messages.body_plain:
" the estimates for "i ~ 1 " and  "s ~ 1 " are the implied means which represents the mean i and mean s for the whole population,"

Correct, assuming the model is properly specified--i.e., growth in the population is linear with time.

On Fri, Nov 20, 2020 at 9:53 AM xuey qiny <xueyi...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Patrick or other Professors,
>
> I have run the analysis following your suggestions, and I would like to confirm with you some of the points with the results.
>
> My cov1 and cov2 are continuous variable and binary variable, respectively. Before fit growth model,  I set cov2 as dummy variable which has two levels, 0 and 1, and then I used scale function to mean-center both cov1 and cov2.
>
> I fit the latent growth model as this:
>
> # i means latent intercept and s means the latent slope
> i=~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
> s=~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3+ 3*x4
>
> # latent growth model with covariates
> i~1 + cov1 + cov2
> s~1 + cov1 + cov2
>
> I used lavaan function, summarized the fit model and obtained six estimates for "i ~ 1 ", "i ~ cov1" , "i ~ cov2", "s ~ 1 ", "s ~ cov1" , "s ~ cov2".
>
> So I would like to confirm that, from the previous post,  the estimates for "i ~ 1 " and  "s ~ 1 " are the implied means which represents the mean i and mean s for the whole population, is it correct?
>
> I am not very confident with my understanding and would like to ask for confirmation again.
>
> Thank you very much.
>
> Xueying
>
>
>

> > Thank you very much, Patrick.

> > Xueying
> >

> > > > > However, question 3 puts a wrench in things. There is no such thing as the mean of a categorical variable. If the variables are nominal, you could effect-code and then mean-center the effect codes.
> > > > >
> > > > > Pat

> > > > > On Thu, Nov 19, 2020 at 9:42 AM xuey qiny <xueyi...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > >
> > > > > > # i means latent intercept and s means the latent slope

> > > > > > s=~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3+ 3*x4

> > > > > > # latent growth model with covariates

> > > > > > s~cov1+cov2
> > > > > >
> > > > > > From this latent growth model, I could get the mean of i and s, and the estimates of i and s regressing on cov1 and cov2 from the summary of the fit model. My questions are:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (1) If I would like to get the estimated mean of i and s for the whole population with covariates, is it calculated like this?
> > > > > >  Estimated Intercept Mean =
> > > > > >                                                   Estimated Intercept +
> > > > > >                                                   Estimated Slope (cov1)* Sample Mean (cov1) +

> > > > > >
> > > > > > (2) When I calculated the Estimated intercept mean for the whole population from the question (1), how can I determine whether it deviates from some values, for example, mean slope deviating from 0?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (3) If I could use the formula in question (1), how to set the mean value for cov1 and cov2 if they are categorical variables?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thank you very much.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Regards
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Xueying
